text:
That's a good thing to have a GPU bottleneck. Most games are more GPU intensive and generally at 1440p/4k you'll usually be GPU bottlenecked. If you were being CPU bottlenecked then your performance would be severely crippled since it would mean you're not able to get full advantage of all the power your GPU has thus lower fps 

That's why CPUs get tested at 1080p since at that resolution your GPU doesn't do much work so you'll usually be CPU bottlenecked and can actually see the performance difference between different CPUs.

text: @lxxl8156  Hi Lx, I'm really enjoying it. I have a 165Hz 1440P monitor and most AAA modern games run at around 100-120fps at max settings. Slightly older games can run at 165Hz capped with max settings. What games do you play and what FPS are you targeting? I don't notice any difference from 100hz to 165 Hz so I've been very happy with the performance. The only game that I have had any trouble with is Cyberpunk 2077 which runs at ~60Hz (all settings maxed and DLSS set to balanced which is the GeForce recommended settings) with the occasional drop to ~45Hz and occasionally it'll go up to 70Hz. That is a particularly demanding game though and I assume it'll get better as CDPR optimise it over time.

text:
3070 is only a good value due to the 2080ti starting at an insanely high price. 2080ti is by far the most expensive consumer grade GPU Nvidia has ever released for its time ($200 short less than double the cost of the previous flagship 1080ti).

So yes it's $700 cheaper for roughly the same performance but the 2080ti was never once in its existence considered a good card in terms of cost to performance so that statement lacks reasonable context.

You can also say the card is $150 cheaper than what the 2080ti should have been priced vs their history of XX80ti pricing, $700 cheaper than a rip off doesn't mean much in full context.

I still strongly believe this card is actually the 3060 of it's architecture, with the 3080 being the 3070, and the 3090 being 3070ti. Releasing a card under the XX70 tier for $500 is not a good value, granted that is always subjective but comparing it to the 970, 1070, and the 2070 shows just how much they have inflated the price for "midrange cards".

It wasn't hard to get a 970 for low $300, same was true for the 1070, and to a lesser extent the 2070 being the real price inflation point. Folks started looking at the numbers in the name and judging it by that alone, and not what each tier has historically cost.

Paying borderline flagship GPU pricing for a "midrange" graphics card and calling it a "good value" ...

text:
Comparing it to the 2080Ti and say that its a lot cheaper is not really a valid argument imo. It is a newer generation card and if you would get the same performance for the same price it would be a bit stupid to even ship it.
All xx80Ti cards usually have a worse performance per cost than the xx70 cards.
A better way to see if its a good buy would be to compare it to previous xx70 cards by normalizing them over time.
Make a graph where the x axis is time and the y axis is FPS/cost for a specific game. Fit a curve (line or exponential whatever fits best) and tell much (in percent) over or under the line the card is.
I did something similar for all xx70 cards from 470 to 3070 using G3D mark score, release date & cost at launch (data from wikipedia). The result was that the 3070 was more expensive than the average xx70 card for its time. (I understand that its more to it and that G3D Mark might not be the best score to use and that comparing RTX to GTX is in itself a bit problematic, but I did it to show how a better comparison could be done) Look at the chart below. 470 furthest to the left and 3070 furthest to the right:

https://imgur.com/a/qt0e5Sf

text:
Hmm... To be honest. I don't mind that much, or rather - at all, if the RTX 3070 is a RTX 2080 Ti "killer" or not. What's crucial here is how much of an improvement the card is over the older RTX 2070 or even the GTX 1070 Ti.  When these card where new, they sold at a price point far closer to the RTX 3070. The audience for the RTX 3070 are not those people that bought an RTX 2080 Ti a while ago. 
Who could buy a RTX 2080 Ti a while back, will not be very interested in the cheaper RTX 3070. They will probably go for a RTX 3080 or higher anyway (if they are available that is). The REAL buyers of the RTX 3070 are those people that bought an GTX 1070 (Ti) or RTX 2070, and where waiting for a decent, but somewhat affordable, upgrade. If you take that in mind, it would be FAR more interesting to see how this new RTX 3070 compares to those older RTX 2070 and GTX 1070 (Ti) cards. Is it really worth the money to upgrade from those older cards? Seeing these results I would say "Yes of course!", but comparing these cards side-to-side would give an indication how much of an improvement it would be. That's in my humble opinion a bit more interesting than looking if the RTX 3070 can "beat" an RTX 2080 Ti.

Want to hear a funny yet sad story? I actually for a moment beat the bots and not once but TWICE got a RTX 3070 in my cart at Best Buy. Home free right? Here comes the knife to the stomach: I scrolled down and saw two alerts. “Not available to ship to your zip code” and not available for store pickup within 250miles of your location”. I tried pushing the purchase though but all I got was “unavailable for shipping” messages. I thought it was a glitch so I emptied the cart, closed the app and unbelievably after a few tries I AGAIN get a FE RTX 3070 in the cart! Imagine winning a huge car race not once but twice and being told you get no trophy or money’s because of where you located? text:
The answer to the question is that if memory bandwith or size is at question between the 2080ti and the 3070, then the 2080ti wins. In tests and applications where memory isn't an issue between the two cards, then the 3070 matches the performance of the 2080ti. Synthetic benchmarks try to stress the memory a bit so the synthetic benchmarks will usually favor the 2080ti when doing so. Real games don't usually stress the memory unless at ultra high resolutions and with ultra high textures turned on. So for the average gamer, they would get 2080ti performance for a far less cost with a 3070 video card.

As for the RTX 3070, seems the demand isn't as much for this card as it was for the 3080 and 3090. I never wanted to buy one since i already had a 2080ti. Looking at most places selling the 3070 and it shows that it is in stock at all sites right now on launch day even after a bit of time has passed. While the 3070 is an excellent deal, the real enthusiasts in the PC hardware world are wanting the best performance of the current gen and not of the last gen. I believed the 3070 wouldn't have the same demand as the 3080/3090 and I was right. This was really based on looking around various tech sites like tomshardware, hardforum, anandtech, reddit, and lots of other places. It didn't generate the same excitement since a 3070 is last gens performance.

Artificial supply and demand created by Nvidia. Just the opposite of the core definition; the law of demand says that at higher prices, buyers will demand less of an economic good. The law of supply says that at higher prices, sellers WILL supply more of an economic good. These two laws interact together on the actual market.

Keyword, "actual". Since Nvidia is manipulating the supply for the demand, in an effort to keep prices high for an artificial demand, Nvidia should be under US investigation for trade manipulation, clearly.

Scarcity does not exists if the supply is manipulated intentionally and willfully. The demand is NOT keeping the scarcity in-play; the failure to SUPPLY is keeping the scarcity in-play with Nvidia cards.

Supply induced scarcity.

Pure market manipulation.

text:
The only one hdmi port but tv-needs-hdmi + hdmi-vr-headset thing really annoyed me lately.

OG-Oculus-Rift did not work anymore and does so only at the one gpu hdmi port, not with a (working) DP-to-hdmi adapter.
4K HDR tv *only* works with windows HDR function on the same single hdmi port, also not with DP-to-HDMI adapter (adapter = no hdr option).

Problem:
When enabling win10-hdr for the 4K tv and then unplug TV and plugging in the headset on the fly instead, win10 effs up.
The oculus does not work at all, everything is supposed to work, hardware detection is fine and all, but you only get a blackscreen.

After nvidia driver blaming, then oculus rift blaming (hardware or broken cable/plugs?)
I found the oculus works perfectly on another cubbled together system out of old parts.

Turns out it was the stupid win10-hdr option:
To change resolution in a "working at all way", you have to manually disable the hdr option, then change resolution (even with the same monitr/tv) then reapply "HDR On".
If you unplug the TV (with hdr on) and simply plug in the headset (or perhaps different screen),
windows tries to change the resolution while keeping hdr-on.. and that simply does not work.

author: @SonOfZeusGaming

text:
TBH, it probably would make zero difference either way.  Cable gauge and pin current rating are all determined based on max load and acceptable temperature rise over ambient.

So, if you use the 3080 cable on a 3070, there isn't likely to be any difference at all because the 1x8-pin adapter will be spec'd to provide all the anticipated current need, plus some healthy margin to avoid even the potential for problems down the line.  There's likely to be 1.5x to 2x margin before the cable even gets warm to the touch.

Part of engineering the right cable and connectors is anticipating failure or degradation of contacts, so there's going to be excess built-in to account for that, which means no particular advantage to over-doing it even more.  Sorry.

In the reverse (using a 3070 cable on a 3080), it's probably still within the reasonable operating threshold, but it might drop a little voltage and get warm.  I would not expect them to be pushing the limits far enough that going from 12 conductors to 8 would result in flames -- that's not much overhead.  But it is certainly ill-advised.

Remember, the 2x8-pin vs 1x8-pin is also helping to overcome any limitations in the wiring up TO the adapter.  So, if someone's running a cheapo PSU with crappy connectors and 18-gauge aluminum wire, it still has a chance of working properly without heating the PSU wiring.

author: @philliumo

text:
No.  The number of pins is basically a safety feature.  The card will draw what it needs to draw, and the load needs to be distributed across a certain amount of copper to prevent the cabling and contact resistance from generating substantial heat.  If you pull too much current through too small of a wire, or not enough contact surface area in the plug, then there's excessive resistance, which causes voltage drop along the conductor, which manifests in heat.  Just ask your stove -- an intentional application of resistance in a conductor.

"But bins and voltage and stuff!"  The power controller expects to have access to a certain amount of current at the card's power connector.  If it pulls more current than the supply can provide (and assuming the supply doesn't turn off or catch fire), at some point of extreme power delivery starvation, it will probably just crash.  The on-card VRMs will fail to maintain a stable low voltage rail, the signal waveforms will look like garbage, chaos ensues.
author: @sirnickity

text:
Does your phone charger draw more currents if you change the 3pin plug to a 2pin one?
No. It won't. A consumer utility will only draw as much power as it needs. No more. No less. The extra ports are there only to ensure that the card remains operational in case it needs to maintains boost.

Honestly, as someone who has owned a 2080ti since launch date, the 3070 matching the 2080ti is the type of generational performance improvement I would expect. 2years ago this performance cost you $1200, this year $1500 gets you ~40%-50%  better performance. It's the same thing as 3years ago $3000 got you a 65inch 60hz 4K with motion smoothing QLED TV. This year that $3000 gets you 4K@120hz, varriable refresh rate, etc. It is simply technological improvement. If you were willing to spend $1200 on a GPU in 2018, you don't care that the performance you got then is now aviable in a $500 package 2years later. Same with the $500-$600 RTX 2070, presumably the RTX 3050 or whatever Nvidia release at the $200-$300 price point will now give you RTX 2070 performance. text:
If there is 10x the supply of 3070s vs 3080s, they will still sell out in seconds.  

A little long-term cost analysis: A 2080Ti bought in October 2018 for $1200 will have cost ~$25/month by October 2022.  A 3070, assuming you can buy one at MSRP in October 2020, will have cost ~$21/month by October 2022.  That' a couple of Starbuck's tall lattes per month.  That's right, folks.  Today's 3070 buyer could have had the same level of performance two years ago for the long-term price of just a couple of coffees per month.  Plus, in October 2022, the 2080Ti will still have 11GB of VRAM, while the 3070 will still have just 8GB.  Given the increasing VRAM demand of top games, a 3070 owner will be in need of an upgrade by then, while a 2080Ti owner might not.
